Problem: Prove that the square of every odd integer is congruent to 1 modulo 8.
Relevant concepts: parity; divisibility; consecutive integers.
Proof blueprint: Write the odd integer as 2k+1. Expanding its square gives 4k(k+1)+1. Since one of two consecutive integers k and k+1 is even, 8 divides 4k(k+1), so the square leaves remainder 1 modulo 8.

Problem: If positive real numbers a and b satisfy ab=1, prove that a+b is at least 2.
Relevant concepts: nonnegative squares; equality case.
Proof blueprint: The square of a-b is nonnegative, so a squared plus b squared is at least 2ab. Adding 2ab and using ab=1 yields (a+b)^2 at least 4. Positivity lets us take square roots. Equality occurs exactly when a=b=1.

Problem: Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Relevant concepts: contradiction; divisibility; constructive witness.
Proof blueprint: Assume only finitely many primes exist and multiply all of them, then add one. Every listed prime leaves remainder one when dividing this new number, yet every integer greater than one has a prime divisor. That divisor is absent from the list, a contradiction.

Problem: Prove that the sum of the first n odd positive integers is n squared.
Relevant concepts: induction; algebraic update.
Proof blueprint: Verify the first odd integer gives one. If the first n odd integers sum to n squared, add the next odd integer 2n+1. The new total is n squared plus 2n plus 1, which equals (n+1) squared.

Problem: Show that among any n+1 integers, two have the same remainder when divided by n.
Relevant concepts: pigeonhole principle; residue classes.
Proof blueprint: Division by n assigns each integer to one of exactly n remainder classes. Placing n+1 integers into n classes forces at least one class to contain two integers, so those two have the same remainder.

Problem: For real x, prove that x squared plus 1 is at least 2x.
Relevant concepts: nonnegative squares; rearrangement.
Proof blueprint: Rearrange the desired inequality as x squared minus 2x plus 1 at least zero. The left side is (x-1) squared, which is nonnegative. Equality occurs at x=1.

Problem: Prove that the product of three consecutive integers is divisible by 6.
Relevant concepts: residues; parity; divisibility.
Proof blueprint: Among three consecutive integers one is divisible by 3. Among any two consecutive integers one is even, so the product is also divisible by 2. Since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6.

Problem: If an integer is divisible by 6, prove it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
Relevant concepts: divisibility; factorization.
Proof blueprint: Write the integer as 6k. Since 6k=2(3k), it is divisible by 2; since 6k=3(2k), it is divisible by 3.

Problem: Prove that a finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves.
Relevant concepts: longest path; contradiction.
Proof blueprint: Choose a longest simple path. If either endpoint had another neighbor outside the path, the path could be extended. It cannot have another neighbor on the path without creating a cycle. Therefore each endpoint has degree one, giving two distinct leaves.

Problem: Show that the arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is at least their geometric mean.
Relevant concepts: nonnegative squares; substitution.
Proof blueprint: The square of the difference of the square roots is nonnegative. Expanding gives a+b at least 2 times the square root of ab. Divide by two. Equality holds when the square roots, and hence the numbers, are equal.

Problem: Prove that if n squared is even, then n is even.
Relevant concepts: contrapositive; parity.
Proof blueprint: Prove the contrapositive. If n is odd, write n=2k+1. Its square is 4k(k+1)+1 and is odd. Therefore an even square cannot come from an odd integer, so n must be even.

Problem: Prove that every integer greater than one has a prime divisor.
Relevant concepts: least counterexample; factorization.
Proof blueprint: Suppose a counterexample exists and choose the least one m. It is not prime, so m=ab with 1<a<m. By minimality a has a prime divisor, and that prime also divides m, contradicting that m has no prime divisor.

Problem: Show that a polynomial of degree d over a field has at most d distinct roots unless it is zero.
Relevant concepts: factor theorem; induction on degree.
Proof blueprint: Induct on d. If there is no root, the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose a root r and factor the polynomial as (x-r)q. Every other distinct root is a root of q, whose degree is d-1, so there are at most d-1 others.

Problem: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
Relevant concepts: vectors; midpoint.
Proof blueprint: Represent three vertices by vectors A, B, and D, so the fourth is C=B+D-A. The midpoint of AC is (A+C)/2=(B+D)/2, which is also the midpoint of BD. Thus both diagonals share their midpoint.

Problem: If a sequence is increasing and bounded above, explain why its supremum is the only possible limit.
Relevant concepts: supremum; epsilon argument; monotonicity.
Proof blueprint: Let s be the supremum. For any positive epsilon, s-epsilon is not an upper bound, so some term exceeds it. Monotonicity keeps every later term above s-epsilon, while s bounds every term above. Hence later terms lie within epsilon of s.

Problem: Prove that the sum of two rational numbers is rational.
Relevant concepts: rational representation; common denominator.
Proof blueprint: Write the numbers as a/b and c/d with nonzero denominators. Their sum is (ad+bc)/(bd), whose numerator and denominator are integers and whose denominator is nonzero.
